title: Alcohol Tolerance: How It Works, Why It Changes, How to Reset It
excerpt: What alcohol tolerance really is, the difference between metabolic and functional tolerance, why some people get drunk easily, how long tolerance takes to drop, and where tolerance ends and dependence begins.
metaDescription: What alcohol tolerance is, metabolic vs functional tolerance, why yours is high or low, how long it takes to go down, and when it signals dependence.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol tolerance means you need more alcohol to feel the same effects you used to get from less. It comes in two main kinds. **Metabolic tolerance** means your liver clears alcohol a bit faster. **Functional tolerance** means your brain has adapted so you *act* less drunk at the same blood alcohol level. The catch is that tolerance changes how drunk you feel and look, not how much alcohol is in your blood. Your reaction time, judgment, liver, and legal blood alcohol level are still affected. A high tolerance is not a sign that your body "handles" alcohol well. More often it's a sign that you've been drinking enough, often enough, for your body to start adjusting.

**The quick points:** Tolerance builds with regular drinking and fades when you cut back, usually over days to a few weeks. There's no safe or useful way to "build" tolerance on purpose. If you need noticeably more to feel anything, or you feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop, that's worth paying attention to and worth mentioning to a doctor.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research about how the body adapts to alcohol. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health. **Talk to a doctor if** you've noticed you need much more alcohol to feel its effects, you feel shaky, sweaty, nauseous, anxious, or unable to sleep when you go without a drink, or you're thinking about cutting back after drinking heavily every day. **Don't stop suddenly on your own after a long stretch of heavy daily drinking.** Withdrawal can be dangerous, and a doctor can help you taper safely. **Call 911 or go to the ER** for seizures, hallucinations, severe confusion, a racing heart with fever and heavy sweating, or anyone who is very drunk and can't be woken, is breathing slowly, or is vomiting while barely conscious.

## What Is Alcohol Tolerance?

Tolerance is a general idea in medicine. It means a drug has a smaller effect after repeated use, so you need a bigger dose to get the original effect. Alcohol is a classic example.

If two beers used to give you a buzz and now it takes four, you've developed some tolerance. The alcohol didn't get weaker. Your body changed in response to repeated exposure, partly in how fast it breaks alcohol down and partly in how your brain responds to it.

This matters because most people judge how drunk they are by how they feel. Tolerance breaks that gauge. The person who "feels fine" after six drinks may have the same blood alcohol level as someone who is obviously slurring, and the same slowed reaction time when it counts.

## The Two Main Types: Metabolic vs Functional Tolerance

Researchers usually split alcohol tolerance into two broad types. The US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) has described both in its educational materials on alcohol and tolerance.

### Metabolic tolerance: your liver clears it a little faster

Your liver handles most of the alcohol you drink. The main workhorse is an enzyme called **alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH)**, which turns alcohol into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound. A second enzyme, **aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH)**, turns acetaldehyde into harmless acetate. (Our guide to [how alcohol is metabolized](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-is-metabolized) walks through each step.)

There's also a backup system called the **microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system**, which relies heavily on an enzyme called **CYP2E1**. With regular heavy drinking, the liver makes more CYP2E1. More enzyme means alcohol gets cleared somewhat faster, so the same number of drinks produces a slightly lower or shorter peak in blood alcohol.

Three things are worth knowing about metabolic tolerance:

- **The effect is modest.** It doesn't let you drink twice as much safely. It shaves some time off how long alcohol stays in your blood.
- **It has side effects.** Boosted CYP2E1 also processes certain medicines, including acetaminophen, in ways that can create more toxic by-products. That's one reason regular heavy drinkers are warned about Tylenol (see our page on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol)). CYP2E1 activity also generates reactive oxygen molecules that stress liver cells.
- **It doesn't protect your liver.** Clearing alcohol faster is not the same as handling it better. The liver is still doing the work and absorbing the damage that comes with it.

### Functional tolerance: your brain adapts

Functional tolerance is the bigger and more noticeable effect. It's a change in how your brain and nervous system respond to alcohol, not how much alcohol reaches them.

Alcohol slows the brain down. It boosts the effect of **GABA**, the brain's main "calm down" chemical messenger, and it dampens **glutamate**, one of the main "go" messengers (acting through receptors called NMDA receptors). When you drink regularly, your brain pushes back to keep things in balance. Over time, it becomes less responsive to GABA's calming signal and more responsive to glutamate's excitatory signal.

The result: at the same blood alcohol level, you seem less drunk. You might walk straighter, talk more clearly, and feel less buzzed than you would have a few months earlier.

Here's the important part. Functional tolerance is uneven. Some effects (like feeling buzzed or looking unsteady) fade faster than others. Research reviewed by the NIAAA has noted that tolerance to some effects doesn't extend to others, such as the complex tasks involved in driving or judging risk. You can feel and look sober while your decision-making and reaction time are still impaired.

## Other Kinds of Tolerance You Might Notice

Beyond the two big categories, researchers describe a few more specific forms of tolerance. They help explain some everyday experiences.

### Acute tolerance: the same night

Acute tolerance develops within a single drinking session. People tend to feel more drunk while their blood alcohol is rising than at the same blood alcohol level on the way back down. This was first described by the British pharmacologist Edward Mellanby in 1919 and is sometimes called the **Mellanby effect**.

In practice, this is why you can feel "sobered up" toward the end of the night while your blood alcohol is still high. It's a big reason people misjudge whether they're fine to drive.

### Learned (environment-dependent) tolerance

Tolerance is partly tied to setting. Research on people and animals has shown that tolerance tends to be stronger when you drink in a familiar place with familiar cues, and weaker when you drink the same amount somewhere new. Your body appears to anticipate alcohol's effects in settings where it usually arrives.

This helps explain why a few drinks can hit harder on vacation or at an unfamiliar party, even when you think you're drinking your "usual" amount.

### Behavioral (practiced) tolerance

If you repeatedly do a specific task after drinking, you can get better at doing that particular task while impaired. That doesn't carry over to new or unexpected situations. Someone who has practiced walking home after drinks is no better at reacting to a car that suddenly pulls out.

### Cross-tolerance with other drugs

Because alcohol acts on the same brain systems as some other sedatives, heavy drinkers can develop tolerance to drugs like benzodiazepines and some anesthetics. This is one reason anesthesiologists ask how much you drink before surgery. Always answer honestly. It changes how they dose you.

## High Alcohol Tolerance: What It Does and Doesn't Mean

"I have a high tolerance" is often said as a point of pride. It's worth looking at what it actually means.

**What a high tolerance does mean:**

- Your brain and, to a lesser extent, your liver have adapted to regular alcohol exposure.
- You need more drinks to feel the effects you're after.
- You probably drink more total alcohol than you used to, because chasing the same feeling takes more.

**What a high tolerance does not mean:**

- It doesn't mean your blood alcohol is lower. Six drinks still produce roughly the blood alcohol that six drinks produce in someone your size, give or take a small metabolic difference.
- It doesn't mean you're safe to drive. Breathalyzers and blood tests measure alcohol, not how sober you feel.
- It doesn't mean your liver, heart, brain, or stomach are taking less damage. Organ damage tracks the amount of alcohol over time, and higher tolerance usually means a higher amount.
- It doesn't mean you'll get fewer hangovers. Drinking more to reach the same buzz tends to mean more of everything that causes hangovers. (Tolerance is about how drunk you feel; if your question is why the morning after hits you so hard, see [why do I get hangovers so easily](/never-hungover/why-do-i-get-hangovers-so-easily).)

There's one more reason to take a rising tolerance seriously. Medical criteria for alcohol use disorder, including the DSM-5 list used by US clinicians, include tolerance as one possible sign. On its own it doesn't mean someone has a problem. Combined with other signs, it can be part of the picture. More on that below.

## Why Do I Have a Low Tolerance for Alcohol?

Some people get tipsy after one drink and always have. Others notice their tolerance has dropped. There are a few common reasons.

### Body size and body composition

Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. A smaller person, or a person with less muscle and more body fat, has less body water to dilute it in. The same drink produces a higher blood alcohol level. This is the main reason the same number of drinks affects people so differently. Our guide on [how many drinks it takes to get drunk](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-to-get-drunk) breaks this down.

### Sex

On average, women reach a higher blood alcohol level than men after the same amount of alcohol, even at the same body weight. Women tend to have a lower proportion of body water, and some research suggests less of the alcohol-processing enzyme is active in the stomach. Hormonal shifts across the menstrual cycle may also play a role, though the evidence there is mixed.

### Genetics

Genes shape how quickly you produce and clear acetaldehyde. Many people of East Asian descent carry a variant of the **ALDH2** gene that slows acetaldehyde clearance, causing flushing, a fast heartbeat, and nausea after a small amount of alcohol. This isn't low tolerance in the brain-adaptation sense. It's a build-up of a toxic by-product. See our [Asian flush guide](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) and our page on [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) for the difference between feeling drunk quickly and reacting badly to alcohol.

Variants in the **ADH1B** gene also change how fast alcohol is turned into acetaldehyde. These genetic differences are well documented and help explain why tolerance runs in different directions across families and populations.

### Age

As people get older, body water tends to drop and muscle mass tends to decline, so the same drink produces a higher blood alcohol level. Many people also take more medications as they age, some of which interact with alcohol. If drinking hits you harder than it did at 25, that's normal. Our page on [why hangovers get worse with age](/never-hungover/why-hangovers-get-worse-with-age) covers the related changes.

### Empty stomach

Food slows the passage of alcohol from the stomach into the small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. Drinking on an empty stomach makes blood alcohol rise faster and peak higher. Many "my tolerance is gone" nights are really "I didn't eat dinner" nights.

### Medications and health conditions

Some medications increase alcohol's effects, especially anything sedating: sleep aids, antihistamines, anxiety medicines, opioids, and certain antidepressants. Others change how alcohol is processed. Liver disease, weight-loss surgery, and some other conditions can also make alcohol hit harder. If your tolerance changed suddenly and you can't explain it, a doctor or pharmacist is a good person to ask.

### A tolerance break

If you've cut back for a while, your tolerance will have dropped. This is a good thing, but it catches people out. Drinking your old "normal" amount after a break can affect you more than you expect.

## How Long Does It Take for Alcohol Tolerance to Go Down?

There's no exact timeline that applies to everyone, and you'll see confident-sounding numbers online that aren't backed by solid research. What can be said with reasonable confidence:

- **Functional tolerance fades fairly quickly.** Many people notice a difference within a week or two of cutting back significantly. The brain's adaptations reverse as the alcohol exposure that drove them stops.
- **Metabolic tolerance also reverses.** Enzyme levels that rose with regular heavy drinking come back down over time once drinking stops.
- **How long depends on how much and how long you drank.** Someone who has had a few extra drinks on weekends for a month will reset faster than someone who has drunk heavily every day for years.
- **Tolerance can return quickly.** People who go back to their old drinking pattern often find their tolerance rebuilds faster than it did the first time.

If you're cutting back from light or moderate drinking, a break is simple: drink less, or don't drink for a few weeks. If you've been drinking heavily every day, read the next section before you stop.

## How to Lower or Reset Your Alcohol Tolerance

Lowering your tolerance mostly means drinking less. A few practical approaches:

1. **Take a break.** A few alcohol-free weeks is the most direct way to let tolerance come down. Many people use a month like "Dry January" or "Sober October" for this.
2. **Cut back gradually.** Fewer drinking days per week and fewer drinks per occasion both help.
3. **Count your drinks.** A standard US drink is 14 grams of pure alcohol: about 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof spirits. Many craft beers, generous wine pours, and mixed drinks contain more than one standard drink.
4. **Slow down.** Alternate alcoholic drinks with water or a non-alcoholic option, and aim for no more than about one standard drink an hour.
5. **Expect the first few drinks after a break to feel stronger.** Plan for that, especially if you need to get home.

**An important safety note.** If you've been drinking heavily every day for a long stretch, stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal. Mild withdrawal can mean shakiness, sweating, anxiety, nausea, a fast heartbeat, and trouble sleeping. Severe withdrawal can include seizures, hallucinations, and a dangerous condition called delirium tremens. This isn't something to tough out. A doctor can help you cut back safely, sometimes with medication. If that sounds like your situation, call your doctor before you stop.

## Can You Build Alcohol Tolerance? (And Should You?)

People search for how to build tolerance before a wedding, a work trip, or a college semester. The honest answer is that you can, by drinking more and more often, and that it's a bad idea.

- **Building tolerance means drinking more.** There's no shortcut. The only thing that builds tolerance is repeated exposure to alcohol.
- **It doesn't make you safer.** You'll feel less drunk at the same blood alcohol level, which makes it easier to overshoot, drive when you shouldn't, or miss the signs of trouble.
- **It raises your total alcohol intake.** That's what drives long-term risks to the liver, heart, brain, and more.
- **It's tied to dependence.** Tolerance and dependence develop through overlapping brain changes.

If your goal is to keep up with others or to avoid getting sloppy at an event, the better approach is the opposite: pace yourself, eat a real meal beforehand, alternate with water, and decide your limit in advance. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Tolerance vs Dependence: Where the Line Is

Tolerance and dependence are related but not the same thing.

- **Tolerance** means you need more alcohol to get the same effect.
- **Physical dependence** means your body has adapted so much that it struggles to function normally without alcohol. When alcohol is removed, withdrawal symptoms appear.

The same brain adjustments that create functional tolerance can lead to dependence. When your brain has turned down its calming signals and turned up its excitatory signals to offset alcohol, taking the alcohol away leaves it over-excited. That's what withdrawal is.

Tolerance alone doesn't mean you're dependent or that you have a drinking problem. But a few signs are worth taking seriously:

- You need noticeably more alcohol to feel anything than you did a few months ago.
- You feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or nauseous in the morning or when you go a day without drinking.
- You drink to feel normal rather than to feel buzzed.
- You've tried to cut back and found it harder than you expected.

If several of these sound familiar, talk to your doctor. That's a normal medical conversation, and they can help you decide what, if anything, needs to change. In the US, the free SAMHSA National Helpline (**1-800-662-4357**) is open around the clock and can point you to local resources if you'd prefer to start there.

## Does Tolerance Affect Your Blood Alcohol Level or Driving?

This is the most important practical point on this page.

**Tolerance has little effect on your blood alcohol concentration (BAC).** Metabolic tolerance can lower it slightly or shorten how long it stays high, but your BAC is still mostly set by how much you drank, how fast, your size, and whether you ate.

**Legal limits are based on BAC, not how you feel.** In most US states the limit for drivers 21 and over is 0.08%, and lower for commercial drivers and younger drivers. A high tolerance won't keep you under it.

**Impairment can be present when you feel fine.** Because functional tolerance is uneven, you may feel steady while your reaction time, attention, and judgment are still affected. Add acute tolerance (feeling more sober as the night goes on) and it becomes easy to talk yourself into driving.

The safe rule doesn't change with tolerance: if you've been drinking, don't drive. For a rough sense of how long alcohol takes to clear, see our guide on [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up).

## Does Higher Tolerance Mean Fewer Hangovers?

Not really. Hangovers are driven by the total amount of alcohol you drink and what it does to your body: acetaldehyde, disrupted sleep, inflammation, dehydration, low blood sugar, and irritation of the stomach. Tolerance doesn't remove any of those.

In practice, people with a high tolerance often drink more to reach the same effect, which tends to make hangovers worse, not better. Some regular heavy drinkers report fewer classic hangovers, but feeling unwell when you *don't* drink is a separate warning sign. Morning shakiness, sweating, or anxiety that improves after a drink can be early withdrawal rather than a hangover, and it's worth discussing with a doctor.

## Tolerance and Blackouts

A high tolerance can make blackouts more likely, not less. Blackouts happen when blood alcohol rises high enough, fast enough, to stop the brain from forming new memories. Because tolerant drinkers feel less drunk, they may keep drinking past the point where memory formation breaks down, while still walking and talking normally. Friends may not notice anything is wrong. Our page on [blackout drunk](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) covers what's happening and when to worry.

## Where Supplements Fit (and Where They Don't)

You'll find supplements marketed with promises about "boosting alcohol tolerance." Be skeptical of that framing. Nothing you can buy makes it safe to drink more, and anything that made you feel less drunk at the same blood alcohol level would carry the same risks as tolerance itself.

Some people do use supplements to support their body around occasional social drinking. Here's an honest view of the most common one:

- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound found in Japanese raisin tree extract. Lab and animal studies, including a widely cited 2012 study in rats published in the *Journal of Neuroscience*, found it affected how alcohol acts on GABA receptors and on markers of alcohol metabolism. Human evidence is still limited. There is no good evidence that DHM keeps you sober, lowers your blood alcohol level enough to matter, or makes it safe to drive. It doesn't change any of the safety points on this page. If you want to try it as part of a sensible drinking routine, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

For a wider look at popular "tolerance" claims and what the research actually supports, see our breakdown of [science-based strategies around alcohol tolerance](/never-hungover/biohacking-alcohol-tolerance-science-based-strategies-2025).

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol tolerance means you need more alcohol to feel the same effect. It's mostly your brain adapting (functional tolerance), with a smaller boost in how fast your liver clears alcohol (metabolic tolerance).
- Tolerance changes how drunk you feel and look, not how much alcohol is in your blood. It doesn't make you safer to drive or protect your organs.
- Low tolerance is usually explained by body size, sex, genetics, age, an empty stomach, medications, or a recent break from drinking.
- Tolerance goes down when you drink less, often noticeably within a week or two, and builds back quickly if you return to old habits.
- Trying to build tolerance on purpose means drinking more, with no real upside.
- If you feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you go without alcohol, talk to a doctor, and don't stop suddenly after a long stretch of heavy daily drinking.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is alcohol tolerance?**

Alcohol tolerance is when you need more alcohol to feel the same effects you used to get from less. It develops with regular drinking. Most of it comes from your brain adapting to alcohol (functional tolerance), with a smaller part from your liver clearing alcohol a little faster (metabolic tolerance). Tolerance changes how drunk you feel, not how much alcohol is in your blood.

**What's the difference between metabolic and functional tolerance?**

Metabolic tolerance happens in the liver: regular heavy drinking increases enzymes such as CYP2E1, so alcohol is cleared somewhat faster. Functional tolerance happens in the brain: nerve cells adjust to alcohol's slowing effect, so you seem and feel less drunk at the same blood alcohol level. Functional tolerance is usually the bigger and more noticeable of the two.

**How long does it take for alcohol tolerance to go down?**

There's no exact timeline for everyone. Many people notice their tolerance dropping within a week or two of cutting back significantly, and it continues to fall over the following weeks. The longer and heavier someone has been drinking, the longer it can take. If you've been drinking heavily every day, talk to a doctor before stopping, because sudden withdrawal can be dangerous.

**Why do I get drunk so easily?**

Common reasons include a smaller body size, being female, drinking on an empty stomach, getting older, certain medications, a recent break from drinking, and genetics. Some people, especially many of East Asian descent, carry gene variants that slow the breakdown of acetaldehyde, which causes flushing and feeling unwell quickly. If your tolerance changed suddenly for no clear reason, ask a doctor or pharmacist.

**Does a high tolerance mean I can drive after drinking?**

No. Tolerance has little effect on your blood alcohol level, and legal limits are based on that level, not on how you feel. Because tolerance affects some abilities more than others, you can feel steady while your reaction time and judgment are still impaired. If you've been drinking, don't drive.

**Is a high alcohol tolerance a sign of alcoholism?**

Not on its own, but it's worth paying attention to. Tolerance is one of the criteria doctors use when assessing alcohol use disorder, alongside signs like withdrawal symptoms, trouble cutting back, and drinking despite problems. If you need much more alcohol to feel its effects, or you feel shaky or anxious without it, talk to your doctor.

**How can I build up my alcohol tolerance?**

The only way to build tolerance is to drink more, more often, and there's no real benefit to doing it. You'll feel less drunk at the same blood alcohol level, which makes it easier to overdo it, and you'll take in more alcohol overall. If you want to avoid getting too drunk at an event, eat beforehand, pace yourself at about one drink an hour, and alternate with water.

**Does higher tolerance mean fewer hangovers?**

Generally no. Hangovers depend on how much alcohol you drink, and people with high tolerance usually drink more to get the same effect. If you feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious the morning after and a drink makes it better, that may be early withdrawal rather than a hangover, and it's worth discussing with a doctor.

**Can DHM increase alcohol tolerance?**

There's no good evidence that DHM increases tolerance, keeps you sober, or lowers your blood alcohol level enough to matter. Early lab and animal research looked at how DHM interacts with alcohol in the brain and liver, but human evidence is limited. It doesn't make it safe to drink more or to drive.
